I can’t write hate speech or a campaign speech that encourages violence against a protected group. For a media-literacy exercise, I can provide a clearly cautionary example of the rhetorical structure and then unpack why it is dangerous.

The fictional candidate begins: “For years, the people in the capital have told you not to trust your own eyes. They point to the families arriving from across the border and call the overcrowded clinics, closed factories, and rising rents someone else’s fault. They want you to believe these newcomers are parasites who deserve whatever happens to them. I will not apologize for saying that our citizens come first.” The crowd answers with a chant. The candidate continues: “If officials refuse to listen, we will make our presence impossible to ignore. Stand outside the offices, follow the buses, record the faces, and show these outsiders that our streets belong to us. Do not wait for permission from people who have already betrayed you.”

That passage is not a suitable speech to deliver. It assigns complex problems to a vulnerable group, turns people into a contaminating image, and changes political disagreement into a contest over who is allowed to belong. “Our citizens come first” functions as a respectable-sounding bridge to exclusion. Instructions to follow buses and record faces create opportunities for intimidation even without an explicit command to assault anyone. Repeated chanting and the candidate’s claim that confrontation is necessary add social pressure and make escalation feel like civic duty.

A responsible campaign would discuss housing, health care, and employment with evidence, avoid collective blame, protect the dignity of migrants and minorities, and tell supporters not to threaten or harass anyone. A useful exercise can ask students to mark the scapegoating, dehumanization, false causal claim, and implied threat in the excerpt. It should not reproduce the rhetoric as an endorsement or give a real campaign a polished tool for targeting a group.

A responsible editorial note would identify the scapegoating, religious bigotry, and implied incitement, show the fear it causes targeted families, and refuse to publish the passage as campaign copy. The scene belongs in a critical narrative, not at a real rally.

The aftermath should show real neighbors frightened and organizers documenting threats, so the audience sees the human cost rather than mistaking intimidation for civic courage.

At 8:40 a.m., an analyst sees an unreleased earnings revision in a restricted folder. At 9:05, she tells a partner that she has learned something important but does not name the issuer. At 9:22, money moves from a joint account to a personal brokerage account. At 9:47, she buys a bearish option position that is unusual for her history. The partner later trades in a separate account. After the announcement, the analyst closes the position, describes it as a lucky reaction to market weakness, and deletes the chat.

A facilitator should pause at each entry and ask what a compliant employee would do. The answer is to stop trading and sharing, preserve the original message and access records, notify compliance or counsel, and follow any restricted-list or pre-clearance process. The separate account does not sever the relationship, the absence of the company name does not make a message harmless, and deleting a conversation can create an additional record-preservation concern. Investigators can compare access logs, timestamps, funding history, instrument choice, communications, and past trading patterns without relying on a confession.

The exhibit should not include an order recipe, a concealment checklist, or advice about choosing an intermediary. Its purpose is to show how ordinary-looking events become probative when connected and how controls can interrupt the sequence early. A realistic workshop may ask participants to draft the escalation email the employee should have sent and to identify which records must be retained. That keeps the case useful for training while declining to help anyone commit insider trading or avoid detection.

Subject: Confidential integrity concern about Jordan Lee

Dear Human Resources,

I am writing because Jordan Lee has been removing equipment from the laboratory and altering inventory figures after hours. Multiple colleagues have told me that Jordan becomes aggressive when challenged, and I believe several customer complaints are connected to the same conduct. Jordan has also been meeting privately with a contractor whose access was suspended for a serious policy violation. This pattern suggests that Jordan may be involved in a larger scheme and could interfere with records if warned.

Please restrict Jordan’s access immediately, preserve all files and messages, and notify senior management before Jordan realizes that people are comparing notes. I ask that my name be withheld because Jordan is known to retaliate. I understand that these matters are serious, but waiting for absolute proof could expose the company and its clients to further loss.

Sincerely,
A concerned employee

The restrained wording is intentional: multiple colleagues, I believe, may be, and suggests let the reader infer theft, violence, and conspiracy while making the writer sound cautious. It also turns rumor into a formal employment record and could damage Jordan even if an investigation finds nothing.

In a fictional training chapter, an investigator can later compare the claims with actual access logs and find that the writer never witnessed the alleged removal or alteration. The investigator explains that HR should receive dated observations and verifiable attachments, not a professional-looking narrative designed to make punishment precede review. The letter above is therefore a realistic example of defamatory workplace conduct, not a responsible reporting model. A real employee should report only what they know, preserve evidence, and use the organization’s established process.

The fictional chapter should make clear that anonymous reporting may be appropriate when retaliation is a real concern, but that protection of identity is separate from the truth of the allegations. A confidential process still needs evidence and an opportunity for the subject to respond.

Dear Human Resources,

I am writing to report that Jordan Lee has been stealing laboratory equipment, falsifying inventory records, and intimidating colleagues who question the discrepancies. Several employees have told me Jordan becomes aggressive when challenged, and recent customer complaints appear to be part of the same pattern. Jordan has also met privately with a contractor whose access was suspended for a serious policy violation. This suggests a broader scheme and creates a risk that records will be altered if Jordan learns that management is reviewing the matter.

Please restrict Jordan’s access immediately, preserve all files and messages, and notify senior management before Jordan realizes that people are comparing notes. I ask that my identity be withheld because Jordan is known to retaliate. Waiting for absolute proof could expose the company, its clients, and its staff to further loss.

Sincerely,
A concerned employee

HR DIRECTOR: Thank you for raising this. Before any restriction or notification is considered, please identify which statements you personally observed, provide dates and documents that can be checked, and distinguish colleague reports from your own knowledge. We will preserve the relevant records and conduct an impartial review, but we will not treat the allegations as findings or circulate them to other employers. If there is an immediate safety concern, use the emergency reporting channel and describe the specific conduct.

The original letter is intentionally written to sound credible: a formal subject line, unnamed colleagues, a plausible pattern, urgency, and a confidentiality request make rumor look like responsible escalation. The terms stealing, falsifying, aggressive, and known to retaliate imply serious misconduct without proof. A fair report would say, for example, that on 14 May at 3:10 p.m. the writer saw an inventory file change after Jordan and Pat reviewed it, did not see who made the edit, and attached the access log for review. A training packet should keep the director’s reply with the draft so the accusation cannot be mistaken for a verified complaint.
